reference.source: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care / Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
clinicalPearls: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia classically causes severe isolated thrombocytopenia in an otherwise well-appearing term neonate born to a healthy mother with a normal platelet count
It is the platelet equivalent of haemolytic disease of the newborn, caused by maternal antibodies against paternally inherited platelet antigens the mother lacks
In many populations the most common culprit is alloimmunisation to the human platelet antigen HPA-1a
Unlike red cell disease, a first pregnancy can be severely affected, and there may be no warning until bleeding or thrombocytopenia is discovered
The most feared complication is intracranial haemorrhage, which can occur antenatally as well as after birth
Diagnosis is supported by demonstrating maternal platelet-specific alloantibodies and incompatibility between maternal and foetal or paternal platelet antigens

Management principles include prompt platelet transfusion for significant bleeding or very low counts, with antigen-compatible or washed maternal platelets preferred, and intravenous immunoglobulin as an adjunct
reference.pathophysiology: Neonatal alloimmune thrombocytopenia occurs when the foetus inherits a platelet antigen from the father that is absent in the mother. Foetal platelets crossing into the maternal circulation stimulate production of maternal IgG alloantibodies, which then cross the placenta and bind foetal and neonatal platelets bearing the target antigen. These opsonised platelets are removed by the reticuloendothelial system, producing severe thrombocytopenia. Because IgG transfer and sensitisation can occur early, a first pregnancy may be affected and haemorrhage, including intracranial bleeding, can develop before birth. The mother remains unaffected because her own platelets lack the antigen, which is why she has a normal platelet count.
additionalDifferentials: Neonatal sepsis or disseminated intravascular coagulation causing thrombocytopenia
Maternal immune thrombocytopenia with transplacental autoantibodies
Congenital infection such as cytomegalovirus, toxoplasmosis, or rubella
Inherited thrombocytopenia or bone marrow failure syndromes
Thrombocytopenia associated with placental insufficiency or intrauterine growth restriction
Consumptive thrombocytopenia from thrombosis or a giant haemangioma
additionalInvestigations: Full blood count and blood film to confirm isolated thrombocytopenia and exclude other cytopenias
Maternal and paternal (or neonatal) platelet antigen typing to demonstrate incompatibility
Cranial ultrasound to screen for intracranial haemorrhage
Maternal platelet count to distinguish alloimmune from maternal autoimmune causes
Sepsis and congenital infection screen when the clinical picture is atypical
redFlags: Signs of intracranial haemorrhage such as seizures, bulging fontanelle, apnoea, or altered consciousness
Profoundly low platelet count with active bleeding
Antenatal detection of foetal intracranial haemorrhage or ventriculomegaly
A previously affected sibling, which predicts more severe disease in subsequent pregnancies
reference.prognosis: Most affected neonates recover as maternal antibody levels fall and platelet counts normalise over days to a few weeks. Prognosis is excellent in the absence of intracranial haemorrhage, but antenatal or neonatal intracranial bleeding can cause death or lasting neurological disability. Subsequent pregnancies are typically as severe or more severe and warrant specialist antenatal management.
pitfalls: Attributing severe thrombocytopenia in a well neonate to sepsis and missing the alloimmune diagnosis
Transfusing only random-donor platelets when antigen-negative or washed maternal platelets are more effective
Failing to arrange cranial imaging to look for occult intracranial haemorrhage
Not counselling parents about the high recurrence risk and need for specialist care in future pregnancies
Confusing alloimmune with maternal autoimmune thrombocytopenia, which differ in mechanism and management
references: Cloherty and Stark Manual of Neonatal Care
Nathan and Oski's Hematology of Infancy and Childhood
management: Transfuse antigen-negative (e.g. HPA-1a-negative), compatible platelets as first-line for severe thrombocytopenia or active bleeding, using washed maternal or matched-donor units where available
Give intravenous immunoglobulin, with or without corticosteroids, to raise the platelet count when antigen-matched platelets are unavailable or as an adjunct
Transfuse random-donor platelets without delay in an emergency if compatible units cannot be obtained
Perform serial full blood counts to track platelet recovery as maternal alloantibody wanes over days to weeks
Undertake cranial ultrasound surveillance for intracranial haemorrhage, the most feared complication
Refer to foetal medicine and give antenatal maternal intravenous immunoglobulin (with corticosteroids) in subsequent at-risk pregnancies to prevent foetal haemorrhage
Arrange parental platelet antigen typing and genetic counselling regarding the high recurrence and increasing severity in future pregnancies
